content.title: Stating a Clear, Defensible Central Claim
content.overview: The central claim, or thesis, is the foundation of the ACT Writing essay. A strong claim does more than just state an opinion; it establishes a defensible position that is focused, qualified, and ready for development.
learning_objectives: Identify the components of a strong central claim.
Apply the Claim-Backbone strategy to draft a thesis.
Differentiate between a vague assertion and a defensible, qualified claim.

sections.title: The Claim-Backbone Strategy
sections.content: A high-scoring ACT essay requires a central claim that is both clear and defensible. To achieve this, use the Claim-Backbone strategy. This involves three specific moves: 1. State your stance clearly in one concise sentence that directly answers the prompt. 2. Add a qualifier or scope phrase to limit the claim, making it more realistic and arguable. 3. Attach one specific, plausible reason that previews the evidence you will provide in your body paragraphs.

sections.title: Defining the Components
sections.content: A 'Claim' is your one-sentence central position. A 'Qualifier' or 'Scope' is a short phrase (e.g., 'in most cases' or 'for students with limited time') that frames the claim so it is not an overgeneralization. A 'Supporting Reason' is the specific rationale that signals the direction of your upcoming arguments.

sections.title: Defensibility and Precision
sections.content: A claim is 'defensible' if it is an opinion that can be supported with evidence and logic, rather than a simple statement of fact. Precision is key; avoid vague words like 'good' or 'bad.' Instead, use specific verbs and nouns that indicate exactly what you intend to prove.

worked_examples.question: Prompt: Should high schools require students to participate in community service? Draft a defensible central claim using the Claim-Backbone strategy.
worked_examples.solution: Step 1 (Stance): High schools should require community service for graduation. Step 2 (Qualifier): While acknowledging the busy schedules of modern students, high schools should require community service. Step 3 (Reason): While acknowledging the busy schedules of modern students, high schools should require community service because it fosters civic responsibility and provides real-world experience. Final Claim: 'While acknowledging the busy schedules of modern students, high schools should require community service because it fosters civic responsibility and provides real-world experience.'

common_mistakes: Writing a claim that is too broad or absolute (e.g., 'Technology is always better').
Failing to include a 'because' or a reason, leaving the reader without a roadmap.
Simply restating the prompt without taking a specific side.
Using multiple sentences for the thesis, which can dilute the focus of the essay.
exam_tips: Place your central claim at the end of your introductory paragraph to serve as a bridge to your body paragraphs.
Read your claim sentence 'aloud' in your head; if it feels like a simple fact, it isn't a defensible claim.
Ensure your claim directly addresses the specific question asked in the prompt, not just the general topic.
content.recap: A successful ACT Writing claim uses the Claim-Backbone: a clear stance, a scope qualifier to ensure defensibility, and a specific reason to signal the essay's direction.

knowledge_claims.content: A central claim is a one-sentence position that answers the prompt and signals the essay's direction.
The Claim-Backbone strategy involves stating a stance, adding a scope qualifier, and attaching a specific reason.
A qualifier or scope phrase limits a claim to make it more realistic and easier to defend with evidence.
A defensible claim must be an arguable opinion rather than a statement of undisputed fact.
The central claim should be presented early in the essay, typically in the introduction.
To verify a claim, check if it states a clear position, shows defensibility via a qualifier, and sets expectations for support.
A common mistake is asserting a strong stance without providing a specific reason or rationale for that stance.
Attaching a specific reason to the claim helps the writer preview the arguments that will be developed in the body paragraphs.
A strong claim like 'Libraries should increase digital offerings while maintaining core physical collections' is superior to a vague claim like 'Libraries must modernize.'
The 'Ideas and Analysis' score on the ACT Writing test is directly influenced by the clarity and complexity of the central claim.
Phrases like 'in most circumstances' or 'for specific populations' serve as qualifiers that frame a claim's scope.
A central claim must directly answer the specific prompt provided rather than discussing the general topic broadly.

items.stem:
ACT WRITING PRACTICE: Public Transit and Flexible Routes

Cities are considering whether buses should follow fixed routes or adjust routes in real time based on rider demand.

Perspective 1: Institutions should adopt the option that produces the greatest measurable efficiency and access.
Perspective 2: Decisions should protect human relationships, local character, and individual judgment even when doing so is less efficient.
Perspective 3: A flexible policy with transparent safeguards can combine the strongest features of both approaches.

Write a unified, coherent essay in which you evaluate multiple perspectives on the issue and develop your own perspective. Explain the relationship between your perspective and at least one other perspective. Support your ideas with reasoning and examples.
items.correctAnswer: Scored holistically with the four ACT Writing domains
items.explanation: A strong response states a defensible position, engages at least one supplied perspective, develops reasoning and examples, organizes ideas coherently, and controls language and conventions.

videoLesson.title: State a Defensible Central Claim
videoLesson.description: Recognize a concise thesis sentence that directly answers the prompt and signals purpose. Use the Claim-Backbone writing moves: state stance, add a scope qualifier, and attach one specific reason.
